title: Digital exclusion is shifting from a network-coverage problem toward affordability, skills, safety, relevance, and gendered use barriers
source_unit: World Bank Gender Data Portal, Beyond Coverage: Closing Gaps in Digital Access and Use in Low- and Middle-Income Countries, published 5 May 2026
geography: Low- and middle-income countries, with Global Findex Digital Connectivity Tracker 2025 evidence from 123 LMICs and an 81-country usage-gap sample

observations.period: 2024–2025 data context; global and LMIC connectivity frame

denominator.unit: global population share in the World Bank's coverage frame

mobile_broadband_reach.unit: percent of world population within reach of mobile broadband networks

offline_share.unit: percent of global population still offline

observations.method: The World Bank data story combines coverage context with Global Findex Digital Connectivity Tracker 2025 data and explanatory analysis of digital use gaps.
observations.uncertainty: The coverage and offline figures are global estimates with source definitions and measurement limitations; they do not establish quality, frequency, or meaningfulness of use.
observations.subgroup: People without Internet use, rural populations, women, low-income households, people with low digital literacy, and communities lacking relevant content or safe access.
observations.counterinterpretation: Near-universal network reach can coexist with real exclusion because coverage is only one condition of participation.

denominator.unit: low- and middle-income countries in the Global Findex Digital Connectivity Tracker frame

countries_with_use_gap.unit: LMICs in which the story reports approximately 1.4 billion adults do not use the Internet

nonusers.unit: adults not using the Internet in those 81 LMICs, approximately

adult_share.unit: percent of adults in those countries not using the Internet, approximately

women_nonusers.unit: women among the approximately 1.4 billion nonusers

observations.method: The World Bank uses cross-country connectivity and Internet-use data to distinguish network coverage from actual use.
observations.uncertainty: The cross-country estimates do not identify individual reasons for non-use, establish causality, or measure the quality and consequences of use.
observations.subgroup: Adults in LMICs, especially women, rural residents, people with limited income or skills, and people facing safety or social-norm barriers.
observations.counterinterpretation: Non-use may reflect preference, limited relevance, temporary circumstances, data quality, or barriers rather than infrastructure absence alone.

barriers.value: cost, limited digital literacy, and lack of relevant digital content can prevent people from using Internet and digital services despite coverage

gender_barriers.value: unequal financial resources, lower digital literacy, safety and privacy concerns, and gendered social norms can limit women's smartphone, data, and service use

policy_levers.value: the analysis distinguishes increasing coverage, increasing use, and decreasing gender gaps as different policy levers

observations.method: The story separates coverage, use, and gender gaps and uses scenario analysis to illustrate possible gains under strong assumptions.
observations.uncertainty: Scenario results represent hypothetical maximum gains under assumptions of perfect implementation, not observed policy effects or forecasts.
observations.subgroup: Women, men, rural and urban residents, low-income users, people with disabilities or safety concerns, and communities with low digital literacy.
observations.counterinterpretation: Infrastructure expansion may be necessary but insufficient; targeted interventions can help while also creating risks of surveillance, dependency, or exclusion.

observations.period: 2026 policy analysis; participation and inclusion consequences

development_link.value: digital connectivity is linked in the analysis to financial inclusion, flexible employment, economic growth, poverty reduction, and women's labor-force participation

targeted_actions.value: proposed responses include women-centered public access points, device and data financing or subsidies, digital literacy, online safety programs, and social-norm interventions

participation_goal.value: the policy objective is not merely connection but full and empowered participation in the digital world

observations.method: The World Bank connects digital inclusion data with policy scenarios and targeted intervention options.
observations.uncertainty: The linked economic and social pathways are not a causal evaluation of the proposed actions or a guarantee that access creates equal benefits.
observations.subgroup: Women and other groups facing financial, skills, safety, privacy, content, or social-norm barriers to meaningful digital participation.
observations.counterinterpretation: More use can expand opportunity while also increasing exposure to harmful content, commercial extraction, privacy risks, and unequal platform power.

related_sources.claim: Complementary ITU global connectivity and usage context.
Complementary World Bank Global Findex financial and digital-use data context.

boundary: This record adds a digital-inclusion route linking coverage, actual Internet use, affordability, skills, relevant content, safety, privacy, gender norms, and meaningful economic and civic participation. It uses aggregate cross-country data and hypothetical scenario analysis, not respondent-level digital histories, platform-use logs, causal intervention effects, a complete accessibility census, or proof that connection produces equal benefits.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: The World Bank Gender Data Portal story was reviewed for the 96% coverage, approximately 3 billion offline, 81-of-123 LMIC, 1.4 billion nonuser, 800 million women, barrier, scenario, and targeted-policy claims.
